title: Singing
hook: the one who sings prays twice
tomorrow: what does a priest do after the last Mass on a Sunday night?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus stood to read in Nazareth and sat to teach, and the lector's job came into focus. The line was lend your voice.

At Mass, it's easy to stand with the hymnal open and only mouth the words. Then someone quotes the old line: the one who sings prays twice. The Catechism credits the idea to Saint Augustine. But Augustine, in his own Confessions, argued with himself about singing in church, and both sides of that argument are still alive in the Church today. So did he really mean it?
screen: `MOUTHING THE WORDS.` → `SINGS, PRAYS TWICE?` → `AUGUSTINE ARGUES WITH HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Side one. In Milan, newly baptized, Augustine wept at the hymns and songs of the church. The voices flowed into his ears, he writes, and the truth flowed into his heart. Singing carried him toward God. Side two, later in the same book. He worries that the sweetness of the music sometimes moves him more than the words being sung, and when it does, he counts it a fault and would rather not hear the singer. He even weighs the plainer way of Athanasius, who had the psalms read with so little rise and fall of voice it was closer to speaking than singing. Then, carefully, he leans toward keeping the singing, for the sake of weaker hearts lifted by it. Whether he said prays twice in exactly those words, the sources leave unclear. The Church holds both instincts. The Second Vatican Council calls its musical tradition a treasure and gives Gregorian chant pride of place, and the same document wants the whole people singing, not only a choir. At its best, side one says: music opens a door that words alone can't. Side two says: keep the words in front, or the song becomes the point. Both treat singing as prayer, not decoration.
screen: `SIDE ONE: TEARS AT THE HYMNS.` · `SIDE TWO: THE TUNE OVER THE WORDS.` · `CHANT FIRST, AND EVERYONE SINGING.` · then, large: `SING IT.`

segments.voice: If you know a hymn, a psalm refrain, or even the sung Amen from Mass, sing or hum one line quietly, as many times as fits. Don't judge your voice; notice the breath it takes and where you feel it, in your chest, your throat, your face. If singing isn't possible right now, listen to one piece of sacred music instead and let a single line stay with you.
Singing. Prayer carried on breath and melody, alone in a car or with a whole church. Today's word.
The line to keep: sing it, even if it's only a hum from the back pew. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics sing hymns, the responsorial psalm, the Gloria, the Holy, Holy and the Amen; some parishes keep Gregorian chant, and a choir or cantor may lead the people.

chat.says: reading went ok!! but mia noticed i don't sing. i sound awful. does it even count if i just listen?
options: Listening can pray, but the Church wants everyone singing. Try it quietly: prayer, not a solo.
It doesn't count. Prayer at Mass only counts if you sing every word out loud.
Skip it for good. Augustine said music distracts from God, so silence is safer.
chat.meaning: Augustine felt both the pull and the risk of music; the Church keeps both and wants the whole people singing. Singing is prayer, not performance.

Augustine.meaning: a bishop and writer of the early Church in North Africa

Confessions.meaning: Augustine's book about his life and his turn to God

Milan.meaning: the Italian city where Augustine was baptized

Athanasius.meaning: a bishop of Alexandria whom Augustine mentions

Gregorian chant.meaning: the Church's traditional unaccompanied sung prayer in Latin

notes: Confessions IX.6.14 (weeping at hymns in Milan after baptism; voices flowing into the ears, truth into the heart) and X.33.49–50 (fear that the singing moves him more than the words; counting it a fault and wishing not to hear the singer; Athanasius's practice of a slight inflection, nearer speaking than singing; inclining to approve singing for weaker minds) paraphrased; Pusey 1838 is public domain but wording not quoted. Confirm.
